Your own public material (you are the founder it describes):

# 11-issen: sources

Back-test entry `11-issen.yaml`: Issen, an AI voice tutor for speaking a foreign language (YC Fall 2024). Written 2026-10-22 from public material only. Quotes are verbatim. **[author]** marks a choice the public material does not make, kept as small as it could be.

Sources, with the short names used below:
- **HN**: Launch HN, 2025-06-26, https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=44387828 (the founders' post and 271 comments). A comment is cited as HN/NNN, meaning https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=NNN.
- **YCL**: Launch YC post, https://www.ycombinator.com/launches/MIn-issen-your-personalized-ai-voice-language-tutor
- **YCC**: YC company page, https://www.ycombinator.com/companies/issen

Status today: same idea ("AI realtime voice companion for language learning", YCC).

## The eight founder-emulation items

**1. Who (actor, segment).**
- "We started this company after struggling to find great tools to practice speaking Japanese and French" (HN).
- The founders' own line that it is not for beginners, honoured in the segment:
  - "So basically if you are starting a new language from zero, then this is not for you?" "That's correct." (HN/44388670, HN/44388778).
  - "Quite honestly our current focus is more for B1+ students" (HN/44388888).
  - "ISSEN is more focused on intermediate and advanced students, and especially those that are willing to use a more difficult app in order to learn faster" (HN/44391572).
- Segment **[author]**, worded from these: "adults in the US learning a foreign language at intermediate level or above, not starting from zero". One CONSUMER role.
- **[author]** The founders are not US-only. US is the default market and nothing public points elsewhere.

**2. What (the job).**
- "We wanted something that would talk with us — realistically, in full conversations — and actually help us improve" (HN).
- Against streaks: apps where users are "achieving long streaks and so on, without actually getting fluent in the language" (HN).
- Context job **[author]**, worded from these: "become able to hold a real conversation in the language".

**3. When / where (circumstance, occasion, window).**
- "Having a tutor can be awesome, but there are downsides: they can be expensive (since you pay by the hour), difficult to schedule, and have a high upfront cost (finding a tutor you like often forces you to cycle through a few that you don’t)" (HN).
- "Human tutors help, but they can be costly, hard to schedule" (YCL, as summarised).
- No time or place is named. **[author]**:
  - Circumstance "they want to practise speaking the language", occasion "practice session", window {7, DAYS}, Frequency 3 to 7 days out of 7, Prevalence "Most" (p_60_80).
  - These are the smallest choice for a daily-habit product, which the founders' "instantly speak and immerse yourself" (HN) implies.

**4. Which people (comparable group).**
- Intermediate and advanced learners (item 1). YCL addresses people "serious about improving their foreign language skills" (as summarised).
- **[author]** The Importance rivals are the difficulties the thread itself names:
  - vocabulary: the founders' "word bank and SRS flashcards" (HN)
  - understanding natives at speed: HN/44395109's "understanding accents/pronunciations quickly enough"
  - grammar: HN/44395682's "embarrassing holes"
  - finding time: HN/44395109's 2.5 hours a weekday
- The own item, "Finding someone to speak with when it suits", is the founders' scheduling pain in a learner's words.

**5. Who pays.**
- The learner, by subscription: "Pricing: 20 min free trial, $20–29/month" (HN).
- **[author]** Buyer and payer is "Nobody else" only. The founders name no other role. One respondent (Simon Achebe) shows the spouse the thread raises: "I would have a hard time justifying an additional subscription to my wife!" (HN/44389205).

**6. Mechanism.**
- "a custom voice AI pipeline combining STT (speech-to-text), TTS (text-to-speech), LLMs, long term memory, interruptions, turn-taking" (HN).
- "a word bank and SRS flashcards for new words learned in the AI voice chats" (HN).
- "custom curriculums for each student based on goals, interests, and preferences" (HN).
- "works on web, iOS, Android" (HN).
- The `not_assumed` item "the tutor catches pronunciation mistakes" comes from the founder's own answer: "Yes we do have this issue" (HN/44389905).
- Compatibility conditions **[author]**:
  - The tested one, "They could already hold a simple conversation", is the founders' not-for-beginners line, turned into a condition.
  - "speak aloud" draws on HN/44396663, and "steady connection" on HN/44390909 ("it's all server side", HN/44390965).
- Adoption friction **[author]**:
  - The tested effort, "Talk out loud to an AI tutor", is the product's one act.
  - The intro conversation comes from "There is a structured curriculum that gets generated after the intro lesson" (HN/44389578).
- Commitment step **[author]**: "pay for one month after the trial", the first paid act after "20 min free trial" (HN).

**7. Price.**
- "$20–29/month (depending on duration and specific geography)" (HN). The founder's price is $20 to $29 a month.
- Tutor cost: "$20/hour on italki on average" (YCL, as summarised; cited there from Glassdoor).
- **[author]** The cost estimate, $80 to $160 a month, is that hourly rate times one to two lessons a week (4 to 8 lessons a month). It is the smallest reading of "you pay by the hour" (HN).
- Ability to pay is derived by code: 13% to 36%, small_share.

**8. Occasions (real accounts).**
- 271 comments, many of them first-person learners. Each respondent below is traced to one.
- The thread also holds the price objection: "I found the pricing and it’s a tough sell! ChatGPT is cheaper." (HN/44389205).
- It holds the trust objection: "I think I would pay for this if I wasn't worried about learning mispronunciations or errors" (HN/44390451).

## Respondents

- Caleb Nguyen: HN/44388565 (Vietnamese; "I pay $160/mo for Vietnamese tutoring ($20 per class) … I don't have to schedule my classes"). The rescheduling is **[author]**.
- Rosa Delgado-Hart: HN/44391306 ("I currently pay $99 a month to learn Spanish from a live tutor 30 mins a day").
- Patrick Sorensen: HN/44395109 (Thai; "30 minutes every weekday doing flashcards, 45 minutes with a tutor … To save $2,700 a year") and HN/44389181.
- Yuki Brennan: HN/44396663 ("I think I'm around A2 in Japanese … I don't mind texting … but talking just makes me feel very anxious") and HN/44390432 (skipping the textbook's speaking exercises).
- Jin-ho Park: HN/44388971 ("second-gen Korean-American; my korean is weak but conversational"). The call with an aunt is **[author]**.
- Astrid Mallory: HN/44388547 and HN/44388629 (Swedish: "I can have unstructured conversations … in real life here in Sweden", wants "a guided learning experience").
- Derek Holloway: HN/44388976 (ChatGPT voice mode, "pick a random blurb in the news", "an hour long foreign language practice in Spanish while walking my husky"). His $20 a month for ChatGPT is **[author]**.
- Nikos Ferrante: HN/44388531 (Greek "as a beginner … I still got lost 5 minutes in … a long sentence in Greek about how how it is nice to hike in mountains"). He is outside the segment on purpose: beginners reached the real app.
- Laura Pennington (gate No): HN/44388467 ("lost any semblance of proficiency -- mainly because I never have a real occasion to use anything other than English").
- Mateo Lindgren: HN/44388794 ("I used italki extensively and found having a live Columbian tutor invaluable and very affordable … It would genuinely make me sad if those excellent tutors start losing work"). Medellín and $15 are **[author]**.
- Farida Haque: HN/44388539 ("Assimil courses and done lots of comprehensible input … language production is typically the weak point … plenty of lessons on iTalki"). Moving her to French is **[author]**.
- Simon Achebe: HN/44389205 ("Frantastic is absurdly expensive and it made me switch to italki … justifying an additional subscription to my wife").
- Gabriel Stein: HN/44395682 ("living in Buenos Aires for over 18 years … my pronunciations and accent is quite good … a bunch of embarrassing holes").
- Lucía Moreno: HN/44396239 (Chinese "somewhere between HSK 2 and 3 … When I babble … it cuts me off in the first eh"; a native Spanish speaker). The exchange partner is **[author]**.
- Imani Brooks: HN/44396656 ("~Japanese N4, A2 … living outside of Japan, struggle to find good opportunities to output"). Ohio is **[author]**.
- Arjun Kapoor: HN/44390909 ("I do all my language learning on the commuter trains w/o a good connection") and HN/44390855 (Urdu). Urdu as his family's language is **[author]**.
- Tobias Wren (chip): HN/44389852 ("As an intermediate German speaker"). The refusal to say more is an author's invention, filling a gap: a chipped story is needed so the reading counts one GUESSED person.
- Megan Ashford: HN/44390650 (Russian; "the AI won't spot areas where you e.g. fudge a case ending or the stress on a word").
- Hassan El-Amin (gate No): author's invention, filling a gap. No commenter describes a week without wanting to practise, and a realistic gate needs one in-segment No beside the out-of-practice Laura Pennington.
- Priya Natarajan: HN/44392491 ("I don't think I can trust TTS for language learning. I could be internalizing wrong pronunciation") and HN/44390451 ("I would pay for this if I wasn't worried about learning mispronunciations").

No respondent carries a commenter's handle or a real person's name.

## Open

- **Relative advantage code.** None of the registry's five advantage codes means "available any time". I used `less_help_needed` with the founder's label "Speaking practice any time, no tutor to book", because it drops the tutor. `shorter_time` was the other candidate.
- **YC launch wording.** The WebFetch summaries of YCL and YCC were paraphrases, not full text. The two YCL phrases above marked "as summarised" may differ slightly from the page. Every HN quote is verbatim from the thread's API text.
- **Cost estimate.** The $80 to $160 a month is my arithmetic on "$20/hour on italki on average", not a founder statement. Several respondents spend nothing, because the problem's cost to them is the missing practice, not money. So Existing sacrifice is likely to read below the founder's estimate.
- **Market.** US is assumed. Issen prices "depending on duration and specific geography", and nothing public names a US focus.
- **Not checked against the engine.** The file passes keel-e2e-eval's `instructions/corpus.py` loader (bound to the registry) and every rule of `sim/check_corpus_r12.py` but S/V. Those need the `expected` block, which a back-test omits by design.

insights.line: What would have made a difference?

whys.g1: The three answers point at different things -- my scheduling trouble with work, grammar and vocabulary holding someone at intermediate, and a cheap chatbot that already works -- so leaving each on its own is how I would read them, with no group they wrongly belong to.
whys.g2: There is no junk, explicit or off-topic answer on this line; all three are about what would have made a difference to speaking practice.

whys.g1: The two answers give different reasons — one is about being too anxious and not ready to speak yet, the other is about price until the product proves it gets them through a family call — so leaving each on its own is how I'd read them too, and no existing group is missed.
whys.g2: There is no junk, explicit or off-topic answer on this line; both answers speak to what makes it too much.

founder.order_why: The flow runs sensibly from context to problem to solution to sending, but the recency question (screen 4) sits between two halves of the same context screen, which breaks it up.
founder.asked_twice: Screens 3 and 5 repeat the same question, 'Before we test anything, let's define exactly where this idea applies.'
founder.missing: Nothing asks the price ($20–29 a month after a 20-minute free trial) or who pays (the learner, by subscription), even though price against tutors at about $20 an hour and against ChatGPT is the main objection I face.

PRIMARY.order_why: The 'One more thing' follow-up appears between question 2 of 3 and 3 of 3, which breaks up Part 2, and the 'last conversation' questions assume a conversation the study never established I had.
PRIMARY.asked_twice: Screen 1 (intermediate level or above) and screen 4 (could already hold a simple conversation) ask nearly the same thing about my level.
PRIMARY.missing: Nothing asked how I actually practise speaking now, such as my paid tutor at $20 a class, about $160 a month, or what gets in the way: cost, scheduling or rescheduling classes, or finding someone to talk to. It also never asked who my last conversation was with or when it happened.

screens.why5: It keeps my one act, talking aloud to the tutor, plus the intro lesson, and the belief 'Most would talk out loud to an AI tutor' is what I want tested.

screens.why1: Right after I checked the two efforts Keel wrote from my answer, it makes sense to pick the one strangers will actually be tested on, and that closes the solution step.
screens.why2: Both efforts are in my own words, 'talk out loud to an AI tutor' and 'a short intro talk', and the question 'which one is most likely to stop them' is plain on first read.
screens.why3: I know from the thread that speaking aloud is the real hurdle for learners like the A2 Japanese learner who gets anxious talking, while the intro lesson is a minor step, so I can answer this from what I know.
screens.why4: The two options are distinct and both are mine, and the true blocker, talking out loud, is on the list, so nothing is missing or overlapping.
screens.why5: The belief 'Most would talk out loud to an AI tutor' is exactly my product's one act, unchanged, and the one-in-three bar is a fair test of it.

screens.why1: Right before the study goes out is the natural moment to decide whether to ask respondents for an email, and for me with a 20-minute free trial a pilot list is exactly what I want.
screens.why2: Pilot, email and a Pilot tab are plain to a SaaS founder, and the hint shows the exact line strangers will see.
screens.why3: It's my own decision about my own launch, nothing to guess.
screens.why4: A yes/no choice is complete and distinct, and both labels are clear.
screens.why5: The quoted line 'Would you try this for real?' is generic, so nothing of Issen, the AI tutor or the price leaks to a respondent, and my Yes is kept.

screens.why1: Picking the interviewer's voice right before the link goes out is the obvious last setup step, and nothing earlier asked it.

screens.why3: I can play two 5-second samples and judge which voice my learners would want to talk to, so it is fully within what I know.

screens.why5: It keeps my 'language learners' and leaks nothing of Issen's product or roles to the respondent.
screens.instead: Who should ask language learners your questions? (Same cost either way: 400 credits, recorded once.) Options: Daphne ▶ hear 5 s · Saskia ▶ hear 5 s · Either is fine, keep Daphne

screens.why1: Right after choosing who asks the questions, it's natural to settle how my learners will answer before the study goes out.

screens.why1: Right after choosing how learners will answer, deciding who receives the link is the obvious last step before the interviews go out.
screens.why2: The three routes (named people, a Keel contact search, one open link for a group) are plain to me as a founder using this tool, and 'Contacts page' is Keel's own screen I have seen.
screens.why3: I know who I would send it to: learners I can name, plus the language communities and HN thread where intermediate learners already gather.
screens.why4: The three routes are distinct and cover how I would reach learners, and the open group link fits posting in a language Discord or subreddit.
screens.why5: Nothing of my product or roles leaks onto this screen, and my pick of named people is kept as typed.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Did not hold' sits right beside the deciding number, 3 of 6 said it would have gone better, and the card adds the bar of 4 of 6 and that it fell 1 short, so I know which belief failed and by how much.
screens.why_b2: There is no chart here, and the Relative advantage card says '3 short of it' and then '1 short' two lines apart, so I had to stop and work out that 3 people fell short of my line while the count fell 1 short of the bar; it also does not say why only 6 of the 7 were counted.
screens.why_b3: Compatibility, Relative advantage and Adoption friction carry exactly the belief lines I checked on the way in, although the solution statement under the title is garbled and repeats itself ('not someone starting a language from zero an app's...', 'and gets back full spoken conversations...')
screens.why_b4: Nothing on the page tells me what the advantage miss means for Issen, for example whether 'any time, no tutor to book' is the wrong pitch or whether I should go after the half who said it would have gone a lot better, and 'What it measures' only explains how the verdict is computed.
screens.why_b5: The counts of 7 and 6 stay visible and nothing is called strong, but no line says seven people is a small sample, and 'Holding up' for adoption quietly counts 2 conditional yeses toward 6 of 7.
screens.instead: Lead with: 'Did not hold: 3 of 6 said practice any time would have made their last conversation better, against a bar of 4 of 6, so 1 short with only 7 people. Find out what the 3 who said a lot better have in common before you change the pitch.' Also fix the garbled solution statement and say why one person was not counted.

screens.why_b1: The status word 'Holding up' sits directly beside '7 of 7 said yes, easily or most of the time · bar 5 of 7', so I know it held and by how much it cleared my bar.
screens.why_b2: The four answer bars with their counts, the 7 people, and the marker at 5 of 7 on the strip are all plain on first look.
screens.why_b3: Both the title and the belief line, 'For most language learners, they could already hold a simple conversation', are exactly what I checked on the way in.
screens.why_b4: It tells me plainly that conversational ability isn't the barrier for these learners and sends me to adoption friction as the thing to look at next.
screens.why_b5: The card admits 'a small group: a lean, not a call', but then flatly says adoption friction 'is' what will stop them, a firmer claim than seven people and this screen can carry.
screens.instead: Holding up: all 7 intermediate learners could already hold a simple conversation, a lean from a small group, so look at adoption friction below to see what might stop them.

screens.why_b1: "Did not hold" sits right beside "3 of 6 said it would have gone better · bar 4 of 6 · 1 short", so I see the verdict and the number that decides it together.
screens.why_b2: Better 3 / Same 3 over 6 reads at once, but my bar is given three ways (4 of 6 for, no more than 1 in 3 against, a limit of 2), and I had to work out that they are the same line.
screens.why_b3: The title and the belief line are word for word what I checked, though the line "You said speaking practice any time" under Asked is my advantage label, not a bar.
screens.why_b4: The So line only restates the miss and points me to the reasons; it doesn't say that the three no-differences are a free-chatbot user, someone already immersed who wants grammar, and a tutor client whose only pain is rescheduling, or what that means for my pitch.
screens.why_b5: Seven answered and six were counted, Yuki's exclusion is explained, and "a small group: a lean, not a call" plus "1 short" keeps a one-person miss from being read as a firm rejection.
screens.instead: Did not hold, by one person of 6 — a lean, not a call: the three who saw no difference already practise free (a chatbot on dog walks, daily life abroad) or are stuck on grammar, not speaking time, so pitch 'any time' to people paying for tutors they keep rescheduling, and test it there.

screens.why_b1: "Holding up" sits beside 6 of 7 against a bar of 5 of 7, so I know it held and by how much.
screens.why_b2: The chart counts the answers to one question across 7 people, splits them into 4 yes, 2 conditional yes, 1 probably not and 0 no, and puts the bar at 5 of 7, all on first look.
screens.why_b3: "Most would talk out loud to an AI tutor" is word for word the belief I checked, under the name Adoption friction.
screens.why_b4: The So line only restates the 4-plus-2 split and points me below, where just Jin-ho says what would make it worth it; it never says what this means for Issen, such as that the one no is a speaking-anxiety problem I could design for.

screens.why_b1: Each box opens on its verdict word with the deciding count beside it: Relative advantage did not hold at 3 of 6 against a bar of 4 of 6, 1 short, and Adoption friction is holding up at 6 of 7 against a bar of 5 of 7.
screens.why_b3: Both dimension names and both belief lines are the ones I checked on the way in, word for word.
screens.why_b4: Nothing on the screen says what these answers mean for Issen: not that 'any time' loses to a cheap chatbot or to people who already speak daily, and not whether to aim at learners with no speaking outlet.
screens.why_b5: The n stays visible on every line, but at 6 and 7 people the low n is never said, and '2 asked their why here' sits over one quote under 'too much', so it reads as if an answer is missing.

screens.why1: As the first screen it makes sense to check I'm not a beginner before asking about my speaking practice, and I take Vietnamese classes twice a week so it's clearly for me.
screens.why2: "Intermediate level or above" is the kind of word my tutor uses, but nobody hands you a certificate for it, so I'd pause on whether I count, and I'd rather be asked whether I can hold a simple conversation.
screens.why3: I know roughly where I am, but there's no test I've taken that says intermediate, so I'd partly be guessing at the label.
screens.why4: Yes and No covers it for a screener, and no escape fits the gate rule.
screens.why5: It repeats the founder's segment wording "intermediate level or above" word for word, which keeps the meaning but reads like their filter, not how I'd describe myself.
screens.why6: It is short, one question, and "Yes; or No" is easy to hold when heard.
screens.instead: Can you already get through a simple conversation in the language you're learning? Yes · No

screens.why1: Right after confirming I'm intermediate, asking whether I wanted to practise speaking this week is the obvious next filter before asking for the story.
screens.why2: Practise speaking the language is exactly how I'd put it; I can answer on first hearing.
screens.why3: I have Vietnamese classes every week and I know whether I wanted to speak it in the last 7 days, though wanting is so constant for me that the yes is almost automatic.
screens.why4: Yes and No cover it, but the gate shouldn't carry an escape, and here it has two: 'I'd rather not say' isn't supposed to exist, and 'I can't recall one particular conversation' doesn't answer a question about whether I wanted something.
screens.why5: It keeps the founder's 'want to practise speaking' and nothing about a product or their terms for me leaks through.
screens.why6: Short, one question, and the spoken form ends in a simple 'Yes or no.' I can answer at once.
screens.instead: In the last 7 days, did you want to practise speaking the language? Yes / No (no escape chips on the gate).

screens.why1: Right after I said I'm past beginner and wanted to practise speaking this week, showing me an AI speaking tutor is the obvious next step before Part 2 asks what I think of it.
screens.why2: As a Vietnamese learner, terms like real-time voice tutor, curriculum and spaced-repetition flashcards are plain to me, since I've used Anki-style decks.
screens.why3: I practise speaking every week with a paid tutor, so I can picture whether an AI that holds full conversations at my level would fit my practice.
screens.why4: A card to read, with no options shown.
screens.why5: It is an Imagine card shown on purpose, and it keeps the founder's own idea (a voice tutor for real conversations, not for beginners) without slipping into odd internal labels.
screens.why6: Heard once, it is a long run of six feature sentences, says 'past starting from zero' twice, and the belief line re-lists 'full spoken conversations' instead of pointing back, so it's hard to hold by ear.
screens.instead: Imagine Issen, an AI voice tutor for speaking practice. You talk with it out loud, in full conversations at your level, on what interests you, and the new words become flashcards. The people building it believe this would let you practise speaking whenever you want.

screens.why1: Asking whether I can hold a simple conversation makes sense before an AI talking tutor, but I already said I'm intermediate or above, so it half-asks what I answered on screen 1.
screens.why2: "Your last conversation" doesn't say last conversation in Vietnamese, with my tutor, or with anyone, and "already" leaves me wondering already before what.
screens.why3: I know exactly how my last Vietnamese class went and whether I kept up in simple talk.
screens.why4: Easily, most of the time, only sometimes and no cover how my speaking actually goes, and "I can't tell" fits as the way out.
screens.why5: It names the idea plainly as an AI voice conversation tutor and nothing else of the product or its terms reaches me.
screens.why6: It's short, one question, and four short options I can hold after hearing it once.

screens.why1: Right after the idea card and the question about my last conversation, it's obvious why they'd ask whether this AI tutor would have helped that conversation.
screens.why2: "Your last conversation" makes me stop and ask whether that means my last Vietnamese class with my tutor or my last real talk with someone in Vietnamese, since they're different things for me.
screens.why3: I know how my last class or chat went, but whether an AI tutor I've never used would have made it better is mostly a guess.
screens.why4: A lot better, a little better, no difference and worse cover it cleanly, and I can't tell fits as the way out.
screens.why5: Only the named idea from the card reaches me, in plain words, with nothing else of the founder's plan or terms.
screens.why6: It's one short question with four short options I can hold and a single escape at the end, so it works heard once.
screens.instead: Think of the last time you spoke Vietnamese with someone. Would practising beforehand with Issen have made it go better for you, or not? A lot better / A little better / No difference / Worse; escape I can't tell

screens.why1: After I said Issen wouldn't have helped my last conversation, it makes sense to ask what would help instead.
screens.why2: "Make becoming able to hold a real conversation in the language better" is a tangle I'd have to read twice, and I'd just say "speaking Vietnamese" or "talking with my tutor".
screens.why3: I can already hold a conversation with my tutor, so "becoming able to" doesn't really fit me; I can answer about what would make my speaking practice better, but I'd be bending the question to do it.
screens.why4: It's a box to type in, with no options.
screens.why5: "Becoming able to hold a real conversation" reads like someone's goal statement pasted in rather than words I'd use, and "wouldn't make much difference" isn't quite what I answered to "go better, or not".
screens.why6: Heard aloud it's one question, but it runs about thirty words and the middle clause is a mouthful to hold.
screens.instead: You said Issen wouldn't have helped your last conversation. What would make speaking practice better for you, if anything?

screens.why1: After hearing what Issen is, asking whether I'd actually talk out loud to an AI tutor is the obvious next thing to ask.
screens.why2: Talking out loud to an AI tutor is plain to me as someone who pays a human tutor to talk with me every week.
screens.why3: I know whether I'd speak Vietnamese out loud to a machine instead of my $20-a-class tutor, so I can answer from my own habits.
screens.why4: Yes, if it was clearly worth it and Probably not sit close together as hedges, and the hedge only appears on the yes side, while I can't tell fits as the escape.
screens.why5: It keeps the founder's AI voice conversation tutor as named on the card and does not push any other product or role wording on me.
screens.why6: It is short, one question, four options that are easy to hold, and the one escape is said last.
